lesson.title: Limits and Continuity: What Happens as You Get Infinitely Close
lesson.summary: A limit describes the value a function approaches as its input gets arbitrarily close to a target point, even at a point where the function itself might be undefined, and continuity describes when a function actually reaches the value it approaches.
lesson.body:
Every function you evaluated in earlier chapters answered the question 'what is the output at this exact input.' A limit asks a subtly different question: 'what value is the function heading toward as the input gets closer and closer to some target, without necessarily ever asking what happens exactly at that target.' This distinction matters because some functions misbehave at a single point, perhaps they are undefined there, while still approaching a perfectly well-defined value everywhere nearby, and a limit is the tool that captures that approaching behavior precisely.

Formally, we write the limit of f(x) as x approaches a equals L to mean that f(x) gets arbitrarily close to the number L whenever x is close enough to a, whether x approaches from values slightly less than a or slightly greater than a. For the limit to exist, the function has to approach the same value L from both directions. If the function approaches one value from the left and a different value from the right, the overall limit does not exist at that point, even if each one-sided approach is perfectly well-behaved.

Consider the function f(x) equals (x squared minus 4) divided by (x minus 2), and find the limit as x approaches 2. Plugging x = 2 directly gives 0 divided by 0, which is undefined, so the function itself has no value at x = 2. But algebra reveals what is happening nearby: the numerator factors as (x minus 2)(x plus 2), so for any x other than 2, the (x minus 2) in the numerator and denominator cancel, leaving simply x plus 2. As x approaches 2, x plus 2 approaches 4. You can see this numerically too: at x = 1.9, the original expression evaluates to 3.9, and at x = 2.1, it evaluates to 4.1, both closing in on 4 from either side. So the limit as x approaches 2 is 4, even though the function is not actually defined at x = 2 itself.

This example is exactly what a discontinuity looks like. A function is continuous at a point when three things all hold simultaneously: the function is actually defined there, the limit exists there, and the limit's value matches the function's actual value there. The function above fails the very first condition, since it is undefined at x = 2, so it has what is called a removable discontinuity, a single missing point, or hole, in an otherwise smooth curve, right at x = 2. A straight line from the linear equations chapter, by contrast, is continuous everywhere, since at every single point it is defined, its limit exists, and the two always match.

Limits are more than a topic in their own right, they are the rigorous foundation underneath the derivative, the next concept in this course. Every derivative is defined as a particular limit, so the comfort you build here, working algebraically to simplify an expression before evaluating what it approaches, transfers directly into calculating rates of change on curves.
